“#Prevent, #Engage and#Act”

These were the three keywords I brought back home from the ReAct Asia Pacific Regional Conference on#AMR 2026, held in Jakarta last week.
 
Just ahead of#WAAW2026, clinicians, researchers, policymakers, CSOs and youth came together for two days to deliberate on a collective course of action for the years ahead.

#Prevent: The updated WHO Global Action Plan (2026–2036) puts prevention first. As one speaker put it, infection control, immunisation and WASH are among the most powerful AMR programmes we have. That means stopping infections before they need #antibiotics. Another session suggested teaching infection prevention to students early, so they carry it into practice and pass it on to their peers.

#Engage: AMR can’t be fixed by the health sector alone. One participant asked where the ministers of agriculture and environment were in the room, and another said the finance minister should be involved from day zero. The session that stayed with me most put people at the centre. AMR survivor Ankita Mitra reminded us that an infection may be diagnosed in one person, but the consequences are lived by an entire family. Civil society, communities, and young people have to be part of the solution.

#Act: Plans are only as good as their delivery. Most plans are not costed, and WHO shared that only about 10% of countries had domestic funding for their national action plans in 2024. The call from the room was to cost the plan, set measurable indicators, close the reporting gap, and scale what already works.

My biggest learning was seemingly obvious: AMR cannot be tackled without addressing the systemic challenges that sit beneath it. Plans stay unfunded, sectors stay siloed, and accountability stays weak. Access to antibiotics and diagnostics remains unequal, and infection control and primary care are still stretched thin. Climate change, disasters and conflict make all of this worse, because every flood or crisis can become an AMR event.
 
Underneath all of it is social inequity. Those who are poorer, more displaced, and further from care are the ones who face the weakest infection control, the limited access to diagnostics, and the highest costs when treatment fails. That is why so many well-designed plans don’t deliver: they work best for those who already have access. AMR is not only a health problem. It is a development problem and a health-system problem, and it needs to be treated as both.

We enountered some of these stories through the #SochSamajhKe fellowship, whichSuperheroes Against Superbugs organized earlier this year in collabortion withYouth Ki Awaaz. Seeing them echoed in Jakarta was a strong motivation for us to continue our work at SaS.

There is still appetite among banks to finance renewable energy projects in Indonesia. But appetite alone does not get projects across the finish line.

Looking back, I recently joined a roundtable discussion at Solar & Storage Live Indonesia, titled “From Pipeline to Financial Close: Who Must Carry the Risk in Indonesia’s Solar Expansion”, led by Ian Leonard Betts, MA F.ISRM, alongside representatives from banks and fellow renewables developers.

The discussion brought us back to a longstanding question in Indonesia's renewable energy transition: as the country continues to advance its renewable energy ambitions and attract investment interest, what will it take to translate more opportunities into projects that reach financial close?

Part of the answer lies in strengthening the conditions that support project development. Clear and consistent policy frameworks, appropriate risk allocation, sound financing structures and bankable agreements all play an important role. Equally important is ensuring that the different stakeholders involved have a shared understanding of the opportunities, requirements and practical considerations of renewable energy development.

Progress will require continued collaboration across the ecosystem. Policymakers, financial institutions, developers and businesses each have an important role to play. Greater alignment between these stakeholders can help build confidence, support more effective project planning and create commercially viable pathways for renewable energy development.

For businesses, this conversation also has a longer-term dimension. Energy decisions are increasingly connected to operational resilience, cost management and the ability to adapt as business needs and market conditions evolve. Having the right energy strategy in place is therefore not only part of the transition, but also an important consideration for long-term business resilience.

This is why bringing stakeholders together matters. Forums like Solar & Storage Live provide an opportunity to exchange perspectives, better understand different priorities and explore practical ways to move the industry forward.

Thank you to CastleAsia/PT Jasa Cita for bringing together such a relevant mix of stakeholders and facilitating this important conversation.

But has anyone here ever actually seen an analysis report for the engine oil drained from their own car or motorcycle?
Probably not.

After launch, we will not be able to analyse every customer’s used oil at every oil change either.

That is why we want to collect as much data as possible through test riders, classified by model, age, and operating pattern.

Once the products are registered and launched, we plan to ask riders about their motorcycle model, riding habits, and average mileage, then use the accumulated data to recommend suitable engine oil and oil change intervals.

This data by model and usage category is extremely important.

Changing oil too early creates unnecessary expense. 
Changing it too late can lead to engine damage and much greater costs.

Some riders may change oil that is still usable simply because a month has passed. 
Others may need an oil change before that month is up.

If we make engine oil with RRBO, there will be plenty of critics claiming that recycled engine oil must be inferior.

That is why API and JASO matter.

They provide evidence that our engine oil meets internationally recognised performance requirements.

And I will publish the used oil analysis results from our test riders after their rides.

🐍 Python Backend vs Java Backend ☕

Both Python and Java can power the backend of websites, applications, and enterprise systems. But they approach development differently.

PYTHON

- Beginner-friendly syntax.
- Frameworks: Django, Flask, FastAPI.
- Popular in AI, automation, APIs and data science.

JAVA

- Strongly typed programming language.
- Frameworks: Spring Boot, Jakarta EE.
- Popular in enterprise applications, banking systems and large-scale software.

POPULAR PYTHON FRAMEWORKS 

- Django: Used to build complete web applications with authentication, database management and an admin panel.
- Flask: A lightweight framework for building smaller web applications and customized backend services.
- FastAPI: Used to build fast APIs that allow mobile applications, websites and other services to communicate with a backend.

REAL WORLD APPLICATION 

- E-commerce platforms: Managing products, customers, orders and payments.
- Banking applications: Processing transactions and connecting services through APIs.
- Social media platforms: Managing user accounts, posts, comments and notifications.
- AI-powered applications: Connecting machine learning models to applications through APIs.
- Healthcare systems: Managing patient records and appointment system

POPULAR JAVA FRAMEWORKS 

- Spring Boot: Used to build production-ready backend applications, REST APIs and microservices.
- Jakarta EE: Provides enterprise technologies for building large business applications.
- Quarkus: Used to build cloud-native Java applications and microservices efficiently.

REAL WORLD APPLICATION 

- Banking systems: Handling financial transactions, account management and secure operations.
- Enterprise software: Managing employee records, business operations and company databases.
- E-commerce platforms: Processing orders, payments and inventory management.
- Telecommunication systems: Supporting large-scale services and customer management.
- Microservices: Building independent backend services that communicate with one another.

3. WHAT IS THE DIFFERENCE?

Python is generally easier to learn and is particularly useful when working with AI, automation, data science and backend APIs.

Java offers strong type safety, mature enterprise tooling and extensive support for large-scale applications.

Neither language is universally better. The right choice depends on the project, team and technical requirements.

MY TAKEAWAY

Learning a programming language is just the beginning. Understanding its frameworks, databases, APIs and real-world applications is what helps you become a capable backend developer.

Don't just learn how to write code. Learn how to use code to solve real-world problems.

Which backend technology would you choose: Python or Java?

Andrew Fox gets the diagnosis right. China isn't dumping. It is exporting the consequences of involution: domestic overcapacity so severe that margin-seeking abroad has become operational necessity, not strategy. The West isn't losing because it is being cheated. It is losing because it optimised for a game China stopped playing.

But the framing is bilateral. Two models. Two scorecards. Who adapts wins.

That erases 150 countries.
If you sit in Riyadh, Nairobi, Jakarta, or Brasilia, the question is not which model is more rational. It is which form of dependency you are being offered, and whether either builds anything where you are.

The Western model sells margin. High prices, IP lock-in, platform rent, consulting layers that never transfer capability. Capital efficiency compounds upward for the seller. You pay the premium indefinitely. The Chinese model sells volume. Cheap goods, supply chain capture, infrastructure financing on terms that look generous until you examine the dependency they create. Scale compounds for the exporter. Your own industrial base never forms. Neither model builds capacity in the receiving nation. One extracts through price. The other displaces through volume. The sovereignty outcome is identical: permanent dependency on an industrial base you do not control.

Fox lists where scale-over-return logic applies. Solar. Batteries. EVs. Then, in passing: now AI. He moves on.

He should not have moved on.
When China applies involution logic to physical goods, what arrives is a car or a panel. The supply chain sits elsewhere, but the product is inert. When the same logic applies to AI, what arrives is not a product. It is inference infrastructure that embeds itself in how governments decide, how enterprises allocate capital, how citizens access services. Singapore's national AI programme dropped Meta's Llama and rebuilt on Alibaba's Qwen. African developers are building language models on DeepSeek and Qwen because the weights are accessible, affordable, and inspectable. Xi Jinping pledged 5,000 AI training slots for developing countries at the 2026 World AI Conference.

This is not margin-seeking. It is architectural. And it is happening while the bilateral debate about who is cheating whom absorbs all the oxygen.

The question that matters is not which incentive model is more rational. It is who is building, and where. For most of the world, the answer remains: not here.
